\begin{theorem}[Noise transition probabilities]
\lean{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF_noisy_apply_toReal}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p254-b008,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b003
}
\label{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF_noisy_apply_toReal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.coordinateNoisePMF, FABL.correlationKeepProbability, FABL.correlationKeepProbability_le_one, FABL.one_sub_two_mul_mem_Icc}
\difficulty{5}
Let $\delta\in[0,1]$ and let $x,y\in\{−1,1\}$. Under coordinate noise with parameter
$\rho=1-2\delta$, started at $x$, the probability of output $y$ is $1-\delta$ if $x=y$,
and is $\delta$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Noise probability from Hamming distance]
\lean{FABL.noiseKernel_noisy_apply_toReal}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p254-b008}
\label{FABL.noiseKernel_noisy_apply_toReal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF_noisy_apply_toReal, FABL.independentProductPMF_apply, FABL.noiseKernel, FABL.one_sub_two_mul_mem_Icc}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\delta\in[0,1]$, and let $x,y\in\{-1,1\}^n$. Under the
noise kernel with correlation parameter $1-2\delta$, the probability of obtaining $y$
from $x$ is $\delta^{d(x,y)}(1-\delta)^{n-d(x,y)}$, where $d(x,y)$ is their Hamming
distance.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Continuous-time parameter]
\lean{FABL.stableHypercubeContinuousTime}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p056-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p068-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p255-b002
}
\label{FABL.stableHypercubeContinuousTime}
\leanok
For every real number $\rho$, define the associated real quantity by $\log(1/\rho)$,
using the real logarithm.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exponential of negative continuous time]
\lean{FABL.exp_neg_stableHypercubeContinuousTime}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p255-b002}
\label{FABL.exp_neg_stableHypercubeContinuousTime}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.stableHypercubeContinuousTime}
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $\rho>0$, if the continuous-time parameter is $\log(1/\rho)$, then
the exponential of its negative equals $\rho$.
\end{theorem}
